docs.preview:
# Contributing

Thanks for your interest in contributing to Diesel! We very much look forward to
your suggestions, bug reports, and pull requests.

We run an active [discussion forum](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/discussions) where you can ask Diesel-related questions and
get help. Feel free to ask there before opening a GitHub issue or
pull request.

*Note:* Anyone who interacts with Diesel in any space, including but not
limited to this GitHub repository, must follow our [code of
conduct](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/blob/master/code_of_conduct.md).

## Submitting bug reports

Have a look at our [issue tracker]. If you can't find an issue (open or closed)
describing your problem (or a very similar one) there, please open a new issue with
the following details:

- Which versions of Rust and Diesel are you using?
- Which feature flags are you using?
- What are you trying to accomplish?
- What is the full error you are seeing?
- How can we reproduce this?
  - Please quote as much of your code as needed to reproduce (best link to a
    public repository or [Gist])
  - Please post as much of your database schema as is relevant to your error

[issue tracker]: https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/issues
[Gist]: https://gist.github.com

Thank you! We'll try to respond as quickly as possible.


## Submitting feature requests

Diesel's issue tracker is meant to represent our current roadmap. An open issue represents either a bug, or a new feature that a member of the Diesel team is actively working on.

This means that you should not submit a feature request to our issue tracker, unless you were asked to do so by a member of the Diesel team. Feature requests should instead be posted in
our [discussion forum](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/discussions/categories/ideas).

If you can't find thread describing your idea on our forum, create a new one. Adding answers to the following questions in your description is +1:

-   What do you want to do, and how do you expect Diesel to support you with that?
-   How might this be added to Diesel?
-   What are possible alternatives?
-   Are there any disadvantages?

Thank you! We'll try to respond as quickly as possible.

## Improve the documentation

We are welcoming contributions that improve the documentation, examples or the guides provided on the web page. 
These contribution are as valuable as any code contribution. So if you notice something that could be documented
in a better way or that is missing an example do not hesitate to open a PR to improve the documentation for all users.

## Triaging issues & Reviewing changes

The Diesel project receives a significant number of bug reports and pull requests. Any help reviewing and classifying these reports are highly welcome. For PR's you can just leave review comments. Otherwise you are welcome to join the [Diesel Reviewer team](https://github.com/orgs/diesel-rs/teams/reviewers) by requesting access [in this issue](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/issues/1186). Members of this team get pinged on PR's that need a review and do have the right to triage issues. Especially PR reviews are a good place to become more familiar with certain Rust idioms and Diesel internals as they are a good place to ask questions about how something works.

## Contribute code to Diesel

We try to keep a number of issues [marked as good first issue](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aopen%20label%3A%22good%20first%20issue%22%20label%3A%22help%20wanted%22%20label%3A%22mentoring%20available%22) in our issue tracker. These are usually a good starting point if you are new to contribute to Diesel. We also keep a project to [plan](https://github.com/orgs/diesel-rs/projects/1) features for the next Diesel release. Feel free to grab any open issue in our tracker or project tracking by leaving a comment there. Also do not hesitate to ask for help if you are stuck trying to resolve a specific issue. Other contributors usually can help you around most problems.

### Setting up Diesel locally

1. Install Rust using [rustup], which allows you to easily switch between Rust
   versions. Diesel currently supports Rust Stable, Nightly, Rust Beta.

2. Install the system libraries needed to interface with the database systems
   you wish to use.

   These are the same as when compiling Diesel. It's generally a good idea
   to install _all_ drivers so you can run all tests locally.

   *Shortcut:* On macOS, you don't need to install anything to work with SQLite.
   For PostgreSQL, you'll only need the server (`libpq` is installed by
   default). To get started, `brew install postgresql@17 mysql` and follow the
   instructions shown to set up the database servers. Other versions of
   PostgreSQL should work as well.
3. Clone this repository and open it in your favorite editor.
4. Create a `.env` file in this directory, and add the connection details for
   your databases.

   *Additional note:* The MySQL tests require MySQL 8.4 in order to pass. If you
   have a different version installed locally, you may want to consider setting
   up Docker as mentioned below.

   See [.env.sample](.env.sample) for an example that works with a trivial
   local setup.

   *Note:* If you didn't specify the MySQL user to be one with elevated
   permissions, you'll want to run a command like ```mysql -c "GRANT ALL ON
   `diesel_%`.* TO ''@'localhost';" -uroot```, or something similar for the
   user that you've specified.

   If you have [Docker](https://www.docker.com/), the following snippet might help you
   to get Postgres and MySQL 8.4 running (with the above `.env` file):

   ```bash
   #!/usr/bin/env sh
   set -e
   docker run -d --name diesel.mysql -p 3306:3306 -e MYSQL_ALLOW_EMPTY_PASSWORD=true mysql:8.4
   while
     sleep 1;
     ! echo 'CREATE DATABASE diesel_test; CREATE DATABASE diesel_unit_test;' | docker exec -i diesel.mysql mysql
   do sleep 1; done

   docker run -d --name diesel.postgres -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres postgres
   while
     sleep 1;
     ! echo 'CREATE DATABASE diesel_test;' | docker exec -i diesel.postgres psql -U postgres
   do :; done
   ```

   If you want to use docker-compose, you can execute docker-compose command like this.

    ```bash
    $ docker-compose up
    ```
    
5. Install [cargo-nextest](https://nexte.st/) via `cargo install cargo-nextest`

6. Now, try running the test suite to confirm everything works for you locally
   by executing `cargo xtask run-tests`. (Initially, this will take a while to compile
   everything.) In addition, if you want to compile and test a crate separately, 
   you can refer to the commands printed and executed by `cargo xtask run-tests`. Additionally you 
   can check `cargo xtask run-tests --help` on how to further configure which tests are executed.

[rustup]: https://rustup.rs/

### Coding Style

We follow the [Rust Style Guide](https://github.com/rust-dev-tools/fmt-rfcs/blob/master/guide/guide.md), enforced using [rustfmt](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt).
To run rustfmt tests locally:

1. Use rustup to set rust toolchain to the version specified in the
   [rust-toolchain file](./rust-toolchain).

2. Install the rustfmt and clippy by running
   ```
   rustup component add rustfmt
   rustup component add clippy
   ```

3. Install [typos](https://github.com/crate-ci/typos) via `cargo install typos-cli`

4. Use `cargo xtask tidy` to check if your changes follow the expected code style.
   This will run `cargo fmt --check`, `typos` and `cargo clippy` internally. See `cargo xtask tidy --help`
   for additional options.

You can also use rustfmt to make corrections or highlight issues in your editor.
Check out [their README](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt) for details.

### Usage of LLM's/AI agents

The Diesel project does not strictly forbid the usage of LLM's and AI agents for submitting pull requests. 
There are still a number of restrictions and rules you as a PR author are asked to follow:

* You need to make sure that the code you are trying to submit can be licensed under the relevant open source license used by Diesel. It cannot contain any code that is i

[![diesel logo](https://diesel.rs/assets/images/diesel_logo_stacked_black.png)](https://diesel.rs) # A safe, extensible ORM and Query Builder for Rust [![Build Status](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/workflows/CI%20Tests/badge.svg)](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/actions?query=workflow%3A%22CI+Tests%22+branch%3Amain) [![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/diesel.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/diesel) API Documentation: [latest release](https://docs.rs/diesel) – [main branch](https://docs.diesel.rs/main/diesel/index.html) [Homepage](https://diesel.rs) Diesel gets rid of the boilerplate for database interaction and eliminates runtime errors without sacrificing performance. It takes full advantage of Rust's type system to create a low overhead query builder that "feels like Rust." Supported databases: 1. [PostgreSQL](https://docs.diesel.rs/main/diesel/pg/index.html) 2. [MySQL](https://docs.diesel.rs/main/diesel/mysql/index.html) 3. [SQLite](https://docs.diesel.rs/main/diesel/sqlite/index.html) 4. [MariaDB](https://docs.diesel.rs/main/diesel/mariadb/index.html) You can configure the database backend in `Cargo.toml`: ```toml [dependencies] diesel = { version = "", features = [""] } ``` ## Getting Started Find our extensive Getting Started tutorial at [https://diesel.rs/guides/getting-started](https://diesel.rs/guides/getting-started). Guides on more specific features are coming soon. ## Getting help If you run into problems, you can come ask for help at in our [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/discussions) forum. This is also the right place to propose new features or show your applications. ## Usage ### Simple queries Simple queries are a complete breeze. Loading all users from a database: ```rust users::table.load(&mut connection) ``` Executed SQL: ```sql SELECT * FROM users; ``` Loading all the posts for a user: ``` rust Post::belonging_to(user).load(&mut connection) ``` Executed SQL: ```sql SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = 1; ``` ### Complex queries Diesel's powerful query builder helps you construct queries as simple or complex as you need, at zero cost. ```rust let versions = Version::belonging_to(krate) .select(id) .order(num.desc()) .limit(5); let downloads = version_downloads .filter(date.gt(now - 90.days())) .filter(version_id.eq_any(versions)) .order(date) .load::(&mut conn)?; ``` Executed SQL: ```sql SELECT version_downloads.* FROM version_downloads WHERE date > (NOW() - '90 days') AND version_id = ANY( SELECT id FROM versions WHERE crate_id = 1 ORDER BY num DESC LIMIT 5 ) ORDER BY date ``` ### Less boilerplate Diesel codegen generates boilerplate for you. It lets you focus on your business logic, not mapping to and from SQL rows. That means you can write this: ```rust #[derive(Queryable, Selectable)] #[diesel(table_name = downloads)] pub struct Download { id: i32, version_id: i32, downloads: i32, counted: i32, date: SystemTime, } ``` Instead of this without Diesel: ```rust pub struct Download { id: i32, version_id: i32, downloads: i32, counted: i32, date: SystemTime, } impl Download { fn from_row(row: &Row) -> Download { Download { id: row.get("id"), version_id: row.get("version_id"), downloads: row.get("downloads"), counted: row.get("counted"), date: row.get("date"), } } } ``` ### Inserting data It's not just about reading data. Diesel makes it easy to use structs for new records. ```rust #[derive(Insertable)] #[diesel(table_name = users)] struct NewUser<'a> { name: &'a str, hair_color: Option<&'a str>, } let new_users = vec![ NewUser { name: "Sean", hair_color: Some("Black") }, NewUser { name: "Gordon", hair_color: None }, ]; insert_into(users) .values(&new_users) .execute(&mut connection); ``` Executed SQL: ```sql INSERT INTO users (name, hair_color) VALUES ('Sean', 'Black'), ('Gordon', DEFAULT) ``` If you need data from the rows you inserted, just change `execute` to `get_result` or `get_results`. Diesel will take care of the rest. ```rust let new_users = vec![ NewUser { name: "Sean", hair_color: Some("Black") }, NewUser { name: "Gordon", hair_color: None }, ]; let inserted_users = insert_into(users) .values(&new_users) .get_results::(&mut connection); ``` Executed SQL: ```sql INSERT INTO users (name, hair_color) VALUES ('Sean', 'Black'), ('Gordon', DEFAULT) RETURNING * ``` ### Updating data Diesel's codegen can generate several ways to update a row, letting you encapsulate your logic in the way that makes sense for your app. Modifying a struct: ```rust post.published = true; post.save_changes(&mut connection); ``` One-off batch changes: ```rust update(users.filter(email.like("%@spammer.com"))) .set(banned.eq(true)) .execute(&mut connection) ``` Using a struct for encapsulation: ```rust update(Settings::belonging_to(current_user)) .set(&settings_form) .execute(&mut connection) ``` ### Raw SQL There will always be certain queries that are just easier to write as raw SQL, or can't be expressed with the query builder. Even in these cases, Diesel provides an easy to use API for writing raw SQL. ```rust #[derive(QueryableByName)] #[diesel(table_name = users)] struct User { id: i32, name: String, organization_id: i32, } // Using `include_str!` allows us to keep the SQL in a // separate file, where our editor can give us SQL specific // syntax highlighting. sql_query(include_str!("complex_users_by_organization.sql")) .bind::(organization_id) .bind::(offset) .bind::(limit) .load::(&mut conn)?; ``` ## Code of conduct Anyone who interacts with Diesel in any space, including but not limited to this GitHub repository, must follow our [code of conduct](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/blob/main/code_of_conduct.md). ## License Licensed under either of these: * Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](LICENSE-APACHE) or https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) * MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) ### Contributing Before contributing, please read the [contributors guide](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for useful information about setting up Diesel locally, coding style and common abbreviations. Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution you intentionally submit for inclusion in the work, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual-licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions. ### Notable Sponsors and Supporters We would like to thank all of the sponsors supporting the work on Diesel. Notable large sponsors are:

NLNet Foundation
Prototype Fund
GitHub Secure Open Source Fund

NGI Zero Core

report.overview: Diesel is a Rust ORM and typed SQL query builder for PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL, and MariaDB, accompanied by a database-management CLI and migration libraries. It serves application developers who want schema-aware queries, model conversion, associations, and explicit database execution through mutable connections. This pinned revision also includes runtime schemas, view nullability inference, Rust migration callbacks, and SQLite examples targeting WebAssembly and embedded hardware.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to diesel-rs/diesel at commit 5cdf54e1434b87084a4630c100249f1028f3e32d. Verify the checkout before relying on this brief. This is a Rust workspace containing the Diesel library, procedural macros, CLI, migration infrastructure, schema inference, dynamic schemas, examples, and development tooling. Cargo.toml declares edition 2024 and Rust 1.88.0; diesel/Cargo.toml and diesel_cli/Cargo.toml declare version 2.3.13. Read repository-local instructions and CONTRIBUTING.md before proposing edits.

Start with the manifest of the affected crate and the smallest relevant implementation and tests. The main library exposes query construction through QueryDsl and execution through RunQueryDsl. Follow load into LoadQuery::internal_load, backend LoadConnection::load, prepared statement handling, and FromSqlRow conversion. Backend features include postgres, sqlite, mysql, and mariadb. Do not assume all SQL capabilities or transaction semantics are shared. PostgreSQL connections own statement and metadata caches; native driver code contains carefully localized unsafe FFI.

For CLI changes, read diesel_cli/src/cli.rs and main.rs, then database.rs, config.rs, migrations/mod.rs, or print_schema.rs as appropriate. Startup initializes DIESEL_LOG tracing, loads dotenv configuration, parses Clap arguments, and dispatches commands. Database URLs come from explicit options or DATABASE_URL. Migration directories resolve through explicit arguments, MIGRATION_DIRECTORY, configuration, and ancestor-directory discovery. Configured schema and patch paths are resolved relative to the configuration file.

Trace migrations through FileBasedMigrations, MigrationHarness, migration.run or revert, and __diesel_schema_migrations bookkeeping. Transactions are conditional on migration metadata. Schema regeneration happens after migration execution, so a locked-schema mismatch does not imply migration rollback. For schema generation, follow catalog discovery, foreign-key filtering, SchemaResolverImpl, formatting through rustfmt, optional patch application, and output. Inspect views and multi-schema behavior when relevant.

Tests and CI were inspected for this brief, not executed. Their existence establishes intended coverage, not passing results. In a separately authorized implementation session, use the smallest relevant backend-specific test first and repository tooling for broader checks. cargo xtask run-tests orchestrates migrations, nextest, doctests, and example checks; it modifies databases and requires a dedicated test database. Compile-failure tests use ui_test, while macro expansion and CLI schema tests use insta. Review snapshot changes and diagnostic expectations; do not blindly bless them.

Keep diffs small and preserve feature gates, public API compatibility, bind serialization, cache safety, and transaction error behavior. Treat raw SQL, filesystem paths, external programs, and example authentication as explicit trust boundaries. The blog example contains a constant password salt and an unfiltered comment update; these are source observations requiring focused investigation, not runtime-verified vulnerability reports. This brief is bounded inspection, not exhaustive repository coverage. Report exactly what changed, what was verified, and what remains unknown.

system_map.summary: The workspace separates typed query execution, code generation, database tooling, and migration management into cooperating crates. Applications link Diesel directly, while the diesel executable supplies operational commands. Backend features select native drivers and dialect implementations, with additional SQLite platform support. Distribution and developer verification are implemented through cargo-dist, xtask, and GitHub Actions.

claims.claim: The root workspace includes diesel, diesel_cli, diesel_derives, diesel_migrations, diesel_dynamic_schema, diesel_infer_query, parser crates, examples, and xtask; its shared baseline is Rust 1.88.0 and edition 2024.
The actual diesel and diesel_cli package versions are 2.3.13; the CLI manifest declares the diesel binary at src/main.rs.

diesel/src/lib.rs exposes associations, expressions, query_builder, query_dsl, serialization, rows, migrations, and feature-gated backend modules; query construction and driver execution are separate module boundaries.
diesel_derives is a procedural-macro crate depending on shared attribute/table parsers and dsl_auto_type; diesel_attribute_parser explicitly identifies itself as internal.
Backend features connect PostgreSQL through pq-sys, MySQL/MariaDB through mysqlclient-sys, and SQLite through target-specific libsqlite3-sys or sqlite-wasm-rs dependencies.

PgConnection owns a statement cache, PostgreSQL metadata cache, raw connection, transaction state, and instrumentation; persisted migration versions belong to __diesel_schema_migrations in the database.
cargo xtask is a Cargo alias for the xtask package, whose commands include run-tests, clippy, tidy, and semver-checks; CONTRIBUTING.md directs contributors to run-tests and tidy.

cargo-dist targets five macOS/Linux/Windows architectures with shell and PowerShell installers, bundled CLI dependencies, SBOMs, and attestations; release publication is gated by the workflow's publishing output.

feature_catalog.summary: Diesel's primary interface is a Rust API for composing and executing queries against typed schemas. The CLI adds database setup, migration lifecycle commands, schema generation, and shell completions. Supporting libraries offer runtime schema names, custom type conversion, and several migration sources. Examples demonstrate associations, authenticated blog operations, and embedded SQLite.

claims.claim: Query composition includes filtering, selection, ordering, limits, and association-based subqueries; construction remains separate from load execution.

The DSL exports insert_into, update, delete, insert_or_ignore_into, replace_into, select, and sql_query; execute returns affected-row counts, while get_result returns the first row or Error::NotFound.
Associations support belonging_to and grouped_by, while joins support related and nullable records; the PostgreSQL relations example demonstrates one-to-many and many-to-many traversal.
CLI commands are migration, setup, database/db, completions, and print-schema; migration dispatch implements run, revert, redo, list, pending, and generate.
Schema configuration supports documentation, table filters, column order, schema namespaces, patches, imported/custom types, Rust enums, views, and experimental view-nullability inference.

Migration generation can compare a Rust schema with the live database to produce up/down SQL; migration libraries additionally support filesystem SQL, embedded SQL, and Rust callbacks or TypedMigration implementations.
diesel_dynamic_schema constructs tables and columns at runtime with explicit selections; custom Rust values can implement ToSql and FromSql, as illustrated by the Language enum.

The advanced blog example offers paginated posts/comments, registration, post creation/editing/publishing, and comment creation/editing; the embedded SQLite example repeatedly queries both static and dynamic schemas.

data_flow.summary: Library input becomes a typed query representation before a backend serializes binds and executes SQL. Connections own runtime caches and transaction state, while row conversion produces application values. CLI input combines arguments, environment variables, and TOML configuration before accessing databases or filesystem outputs. Migration state and generated schema files are separate persistence boundaries.

claims.claim: QueryFragment::walk_ast defines AST-node behavior; to_sql performs a SQL-generation pass, while bind values are serialized separately from SQL placeholders.

LoadQuery requires backend-compatible result types, converts the source through as_query, obtains a connection cursor, and maps each row through U::build_from_row with DeserializationError conversion.
PostgreSQL collect_binds produces raw byte values and type metadata; with_prepared_query passes metadata to the statement cache and values separately to execution.

The statement cache checks query cache safety, reuses occupied entries, registers newly prepared statements when capacity permits, and prepares uncached statements for unsafe or capacity-limited cases.

CLI database URLs prefer explicit options over DATABASE_URL; config paths prefer arguments over DIESEL_CONFIG_FILE, and migration paths prefer arguments, MIGRATION_DIRECTORY, configuration, then ancestor discovery.
SchemaResolverImpl owns catalog-result caching and a recursive resolution chain; requested tables load catalog metadata, views invoke load_view_data, and cycles return CyclicViewDefinition.

Generated schema data passes through relation/custom-type formatting, rustfmt, and optional diffy patch application; print-schema writes to its output writer, while regeneration writes configured files or compares them in locked mode.

SQL migration files are read into strings and passed to batch_execute; successful application inserts a version record, successful reversal deletes it, and applied versions are read in descending order.

behavior_traces.summary: The inspected flows cover CLI startup, database setup, migration application, schema printing, query execution, and example operations. Each trace follows named functions across their implementation boundaries. Migration application reaches both SQL execution and version bookkeeping before optional schema regeneration. PostgreSQL query tracing distinguishes cached named statements from uncached parameterized execution.

claims.claim: Startup: main calls inner_main, which initializes DIESEL_LOG tracing, invokes dotenvy::dotenv, tolerates a missing dotenv file, parses Cli, and dispatches; returned errors are printed before exit code 1.

Setup: run_setup_command calls create_migrations_dir and create_config_file, then setup_database resolves the URL, creates the database if needed, optionally creates default migrations, and invokes schema-table setup/migration execution.

Migration run: run_migration_command calls conn_and_migration_dir, which establishes InferConnection and validates FileBasedMigrations; run_migrations_with_output delegates to HarnessWithOutput::run_pending_migrations, then regenerates schema unless --no-schema.

Migration persistence: run_pending_migrations calls pending_migrations, removes already applied versions and sorts remaining versions ascending, then run_migration executes SQL and inserts bookkeeping inside a transaction when metadata permits.

Print schema: run_infer_schema establishes a connection, reads/overrides configuration, computes multi-schema context, and calls run_print_schema; output_schema discovers relations and foreign keys, resolves metadata, formats/patches Rust, then writes stdout.

PostgreSQL load: RunQueryDsl::load calls internal_load and collects results; internal_load calls connection.load, which uses with_prepared_query, inner_load, Statement::execute, and the selected loading mode's cursor before row deserialization.

PostgreSQL execution branch: Statement::execute builds parameter pointers/lengths, rejects counts or sizes exceeding i32, sends named statements through send_query_prepared or unnamed SQL through send_query_params, optionally enables row-by-row mode, and retrieves a result.

Blog create-post: run_cli establishes PgConnection, current_user delegates to current_user_from_env/find_user and Argon2 verification, editor::edit_string round-trips a temporary file through an external editor, then insert_into returns the post ID.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; no passing result or measured coverage is asserted. The repository combines Rust runtime tests, compile-failure diagnostics, procedural-macro snapshots, CLI subprocess tests, and fuzzing workflows. The inspected tests verify concrete database and generated-code behavior, with backend-specific conditions. This inventory is bounded and does not establish exhaustive coverage or whole-repository test gaps.

claims.claim: diesel_tests registers integration modules for CRUD, associations, joins, raw SQL, transactions, migrations, instrumentation, types, views, and window functions, with some modules gated by backend features.

Transaction tests inspect cross-connection visibility and rollback on returned errors; the visibility test explicitly excludes SQLite because it requires a file-backed database, and the rollback-error test is SQLite-specific.

Despite its trybuild.rs filename, the compile-failure harness uses ui_test against tests/fail, normalizes diagnostic paths/text, and enables output blessing whenever BLESS exists; an inspected fixture rejects integer/string comparisons.

Procedural-macro tests expand tokens, parse the result with syn, apply FixupVisitor, format through prettyplease, and assert insta snapshots; these assertions check generated text rather than database execution.
CLI tests register database and migration command suites; migration_run_runs_pending_migrations checks command success, emitted migration output, and actual table creation.

Schema tests compare CLI/config-generated output with insta snapshots and conditionally compile it in a temporary Cargo project; check_compile=false deliberately skips that compilation assertion for selected cases.

CI defines a four-backend, five-platform stable matrix plus Linux beta/nightly entries, invokes cargo xtask run-tests, skips doctests/example-schema checks outside Linux, and uploads coverage outside merge_group events.

Fuzz CI runs harness tests on PRs/pushes, but cargo-fuzz target execution is workflow_dispatch-only; separate ClusterFuzzLite PR jobs specify address sanitization and 600 seconds, while audit CI runs cargo deny check.

risk_map.summary: These findings describe source-level trust boundaries and review hotspots, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities. Database operations can mutate remote databases or local files, and raw SQL reduces compile-time validation. Migration commits and schema-file verification occur at different stages. The advanced blog example contains security-relevant teaching shortcuts and an update target that warrants focused review.

claims.claim: Source observation: EditComment loads a comment scoped to the current user, but executes diesel::update(comments) without a filter or identified-record target; the update construction does not preserve the preceding ownership selection.
Source observation: blog registration hashes passwords with Argon2 using a constant salt; the implementation explicitly warns against this pattern in real applications.
Operational boundary: database reset calls drop before setup; server backends execute DROP DATABASE, while SQLite drop removes an existing path supplied as database_url.

Source observation: --locked-schema validation runs after migrations; a schema mismatch returns SchemaWouldChange, and the inspected dispatch provides no enclosing rollback around migration execution and file comparison.
Migration metadata read/parse errors are discarded by unwrap_or_default; transaction-disabled migrations execute SQL and insert bookkeeping without the harness transaction wrapper.

Raw SqlQuery binds cannot validate SQL placeholder types or parameter counts, and dynamic schemas cannot verify runtime table/column existence or declared types; these are documented reductions in static guarantees.

Native PostgreSQL execution crosses unsafe libpq boundaries for connection pointers and parameter arrays; Statement::execute includes explicit i32 conversion checks, so preserving ownership and bounds behavior is essential when editing this code.

External trust boundaries include PATH-resolved rustfmt, VISUAL/EDITOR-selected subprocesses, temporary editor files, and configured schema/patch paths; relative paths are joined to the config directory without a repository-containment check in the inspected code.

extension_points.summary: Extensions primarily enter through Rust traits, procedural macros, configuration fields, and explicit CLI dispatch. Backend support separates dialect metadata from connection implementation. Applications can add custom value conversion, query fragments, instrumentation, and migration sources. Internal extension interfaces sometimes require an explicit feature acknowledging compatibility risk.

claims.claim: Custom Backend implementations supply QueryBuilder, RawValue, BindCollector, SqlDialect, TypeMetadata, and SQL-type mappings; access requires the third-party-backend opt-in feature.

Custom connections implement Connection with backend and transaction-manager ownership; the documentation also calls for backend-specific FromSql/ToSql conversions and gates implementations through ConnectionSealed.
New query AST nodes implement QueryFragment::walk_ast, which supplies SQL-generation and other AST-pass behavior; execution/loading requires appropriate QueryFragment and QueryId implementations.
Custom SQL value types implement ToSql and FromSql and derive expression/row support; the Language example serializes enum variants as PostgreSQL bytes and rejects unknown variants during decoding.
Instrumentation extensions implement on_connection_event or use a closure, can be installed per connection, and can register a global constructor for future connections when std is enabled.

Migration extensions implement Migration, MigrationMetadata, and MigrationSource; RustMigrationSource additionally registers callbacks, functions, RustMigration values, or custom TypedMigration implementations.
CLI additions enter DieselCliCommand or MigrationCommand and their dispatch matches; schema customization enters PrintSchema configuration and the Config::read/update path.

SchemaResolver is exported for SQL/view inference, and SchemaResolverImpl adapts CLI catalog metadata to it; table_proc routes table macro expansion into query_source_macro, while view declarations use the corresponding generated schema model.

agent_handoff.summary: Use the pinned manifests and affected crate implementation as the starting context, because the supplied inventory contains simplified version and backend information. Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and this brief covers a bounded set of source paths. Future implementation work should preserve backend gates and use dedicated test databases before authorizing execution. Public API changes, generated diagnostics, schema snapshots, and embedded migration rebuilds require special attention.

claims.claim: Read Cargo.toml and the affected crate manifest first: Rust 1.88.0/edition 2024, Diesel 2.3.13, four backend features, and target-specific SQLite dependencies are concrete constraints in this revision.
For query-runtime changes, follow RunQueryDsl::load, LoadQuery::internal_load, backend LoadConnection, statement preparation, and row decoding before choosing an edit boundary.

For CLI/schema work, read cli.rs, main.rs, config.rs, and print_schema.rs together; configuration overrides, relative paths, multi-schema context, patches, and locked-file handling all affect observable output.

The inspected test sources and workflow declarations describe intended checks, not execution results: review CLI schema snapshots/compilation, migration assertions, compile-failure diagnostics, and CI configuration before planning validation.

In authorized implementation work, start with the affected backend/test and use cargo xtask run-tests for broader checks; xtask resolves backend-specific database variables, runs migrations first, and invokes nextest with coordinated crate features.

Preserve compile-error and snapshot expectations deliberately: BLESS presence rewrites ui_test outputs, while CONTRIBUTING.md calls for reviewing insta changes; tidy and semver-checks are existing tooling entrypoints.
Embedded migrations have a documented rebuild trap: changes only to migration files may not rerun the procedural macro, and consuming applications should use build.rs rerun-if-changed declarations.

Contribution conventions require minimal, reviewed, verified changes and AI-use disclosure; the guide reserves mentoring/good-first-issue work from AI use and asks authors to write their own PR descriptions.
